output:
Inspector,

You will want this in order. I have always preferred a history to an opinion, so I give you the history.

In the winter of 1889 I attended Jules Monnier in his last illness. I gave him laudanum for his pain. On one bad night I raised the dose, and then raised it again, and he did not wake. I entered the death as failure of the heart. The certificate is in the register under my hand. No one asked me to explain it, and I did not offer to. For ten years afterwards I dined at the Monniers' table as their physician and friend.

In December Aurèle was sorting his brother's papers for the new century. He found Jules's last letter, which set out the doses, and he understood them. He told me so in the hall before dinner on the thirty-first. He would tell Félix at midnight and the authorities after. "At the turn of the century I settle my accounts." He said it without heat, which was the worst of it.

After dinner I played piquet with Odile in the salon. At 22:33 I rose for my cigars and asked her to play for me, so that the piano would cover my steps. I had sent Mademoiselle Ruedi downstairs at 22:20. I went up the two flights and passed the library door at 22:35, shut. In the atelier Aurèle was alone at his bench under the long windows. I struck him once, from behind, with the brass mallet from his own bench. This was at 22:38.

He fell, and as he fell he pressed the slide of the repeater. It struck ten low notes, two doubled, and eight high: ten thirty-eight. I counted it as anyone in this town would count it, and I understood what I had done.

I stopped the regulator's pendulum and set its hands back to five past ten, an hour when I had sat at cards in plain view of the salon. I did not think beyond that. I came down at 22:41, took the cigar case from my coat in the hall, and was back in the salon at 22:46. Odile stopped playing when I came in. The hall clock struck eleven a moment later.

I told you I left the salon at a quarter to eleven by my watch. My watch has been two minutes fast all evening, and I knew it when I gave you the time. I gave you the hour at which the repeater would already have sounded. I did not know that Félix, below, and Girard, in the street, had both heard the repeater, or that the kitchen had heard the piano begin. Those were the things I did not reckon with. Everything else I told you is true.

I have no defence worth your time. I shall be in the house when you return, and I shall not give you trouble. Please tell Odile before the others do.

Casimir Vauthier
1 January 1900, at dawn
